extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and critics interested in heroic/epic drama (Restoration-era literary practitioners and readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing or judging heroic poems and heroic plays: their scale, use of supernatural, characterisation of heroes, and theatrical devices to produce grandeur and imaginative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur and a single great action (unity and scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: An heroic poem should comport 'one entire and great action' and raise the ordinary laws of other (poetic/dramatic) forms to a greater height; its images and design must match that greatness and majesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not scant images or design; a heroic work must be filled with persons, beautified with characters, and varied with accidents to suit the elevated scale. The laws of a heroic poem 'raised... to a greater height' require correspondingly larger treatment than ordinary stage poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not merely a play-in-narration (avoid reducing epic to domestic realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A heroic poem should not be 'dressed in a more familiar and easy shape' so as to resemble everyday stage poetry or merely a play in narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware arguments that heroic poetry ought to imitate common actions and passions or be divided into acts/cantos like stage scenes; such reduction risks making the epic only a narrated play rather than a true heroic poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of fancy and elevated representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic poet is indulged a 'farther liberty of fancy' to draw things 'as far above the ordinary proportion of the stage' as poetry stands above common words and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit imagination freely; allow imagery and situations that exceed everyday plausibility to achieve the greater aims of heroic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of gods, spirits, and enthusiastic (supernatural) elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Great epic/herioc poets (Homer, Virgil, Tasso, Spencer) rely on gods, spirits, and enthusiastic portions of poetry which compose the most noble parts of their works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use supernatural apparitions (ghosts, enchanted woods, magic palaces) as important poetic devices—examples given: the ghost of Polydorus (Virgil), the Enchanted Wood (Tasso), the Bower of Bliss (Spencer). These augment beauty and nobility of epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission for improbability when poetically justifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: An heroic poet 'is not tied to a bare representation of what is true, or exceeding probable; but... may let himself loose to visionary objects'—the improbable may be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improbable or visionary elements are permissible if they serve poetic ends and rest on cultural or imaginative plausibility (e.g., widespread belief in magic/spirits). The poet needn't confine himself to strict probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural plausibility as sufficient foundation for supernatural elements
rubrics_metrics.description: It is enough that 'in all ages and religions, the greatest part of mankind have believed the power of magic, and that there are spirits or spectres which have appeared.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widespread belief or historical/cultural acceptance of supernatural phenomena can justify their inclusion in poetry; 'whatever is, or may be, is not properly unnatural.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic speculation can better handle dark/metaphysical problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines about separated beings or subtle metaphysical questions 'may better be explicated by poets than by philosophers or divines' because poets rely on fancy and imaginative insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating unknowable or doubtful matters, prefer poetical, imaginative exposition rather than dry philosophical proof—poets can offer more satisfactory notions on such problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of theatrical spectacle and sound (drums, trumpets, battles) to raise imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Drums, trumpets, and representations of battles are 'no more than necessary to produce the effects of an heroic play'—they raise the imagination and persuade audiences that what they behold is really performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ stage effects and sounds to help the audience's fancy and belief; theatrical devices that make the performance convincing are legitimate even if they are borrowed from vulgar or popular practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama's advantage: showing rather than merely relating
rubrics_metrics.description: The drama 'represents to view what the poem only does relate,' and visible representation affects the audience more directly ('Segnius irritant animum demissa per aures, quam quæ sunt oculis subjecta fidelibus').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting epic material to the stage, take advantage of the medium's capacity to show events and thereby move the audience more powerfully than narrative alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroes should be noble but retain human passions and frailties
rubrics_metrics.description: Great authors made their heroes 'men of honour; but so, as not to divest them quite of human passions and frailties': they display what great-spirited men would do when provoked, not what strict moral virtue would require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterise heroes with grandeur and honour but allow anger, impatience, pride, and other passions (illustrated by Achilles, Rinaldo). Avoid making them morally antiseptic or unrealistically exact in conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject overly precise French niceties about honour and love
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not subject characters to the 'French standard, where love and honour are to be weighed by drams and scruples.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer bolder, less legally measured depictions of honour and love; allow larger temperaments and dramatic excesses appropriate to heroic style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify extraordinary actions with credible antecedents (narrative plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary feats (e.g., a stranger appeasing two factions) may be improbable but acceptable if context gives them credibility—reputation, prior conspicuous deeds, local circumstances, or supporting forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When plotting improbable successes, provide motivating facts: public reputation, prior gallantry, presence of supporting troops, or historical parallels to make the action believable rather than impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use effective theatrical means regardless of vulgar origins
rubrics_metrics.description: That popular or 'mountebank' entertainments have used a device is no reason to forbear it if it produces desired effect ('no more an argument against our practice, than it would be for a physician to forbear an approved medicine, because a mountebank has used it with success').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject a useful stage convention merely because it has low origins; privilege efficacy in producing the poetic/theatrical effect.
